articles.deck: Ali from Cairo — 1994 Red Defense study
articles.era: 1994 casual early-Constructed illustrative table under modern damage rules
articles.matchup: Red defensive study against artifact beatdown
articles.title: Five damage still left me alive at one
articles.intro: Ali from Cairo does not prevent combat damage. Its unusual replacement effect prevents damage from reducing its controller's life total below one, while non-damage life loss remains lethal.
articles.lesson: Damage that would drop the controller below one life changes that life-total reduction to one, without erasing the damage dealt. A loss of life that is not damage and removal of Ali before later damage remain dangerous.
articles.origin: Ali from Cairo first appeared in Arabian Nights in December 1993 with artwork by Mark Poole. Its tiny 0/1 body asks for four mana to create a defensive rule; this is not a claim that early tournament lists used it.
articles.technical: Under current rules a five-damage Juggernaut attack at three life leaves Ali's controller at one life while Ali stays on the battlefield. Damage-triggered abilities still see damage dealt. A separate life-loss effect can defeat a player at one; do not conflate damage prevention with a life-total replacement.
articles.history: There is no verified historical registration in the inherited 073 archive. The added 60-card original study deck is explicitly an authored 1994 legal-card-pool illustration and cannot establish tournament popularity or an actual result.
articles.story: I was at three life with [[Ali from Cairo]] beside two [[Mountain]]s and nothing large enough to block. My opponent sent [[Juggernaut]] at me for five combat damage. Ali's replacement effect meant the attack left my life total at one rather than below zero. The attack still dealt damage; Ali had not prevented it. I needed a way to end the game, and I kept [[Lightning Bolt]] in hand for the following turn. If Ali disappeared before another hit, my one remaining life would not protect me. It was survival, not invulnerability.
articles.review: Five Juggernaut combat damage against 3-life defender with Ali leads to 1 life, not prevention; creature remains live. Fictional opponents, no tournament attribution.

articles.era: 2023 Old School with modern triggered-ability rules
articles.title: The upkeep made me choose between two creatures
articles.intro: Drop of Honey is a one-green-mana enchantment with an untargeted upkeep destruction effect, not a spell that destroys everything at once.
articles.lesson: At its controller's upkeep the creature with least power is destroyed without regeneration; if the least-power creatures tie, the controller chooses one during resolution. It does not target. Once there are no creatures on the battlefield it must be sacrificed.
articles.origin: Anson Maddocks illustrated Drop of Honey for Arabian Nights in December 1993. Its slow symmetrical destruction appealed to creature-light control shells because it made the next upkeep strategically relevant.
articles.technical: If Kird Ape and Savannah Lions each have two power, Drop's controller chooses one of the tied creatures during the upkeep ability's resolution. The choice isn't targeting. The other creature survives the turn; the spell does not allow regeneration of the destroyed one.
articles.history: Odd Anders Kjostvedt's 2023 U/G Control Old School archive includes Drop of Honey. The reconstructed opposing red-green creatures are not documented as that player's particular matchup.
articles.story: I began my upkeep controlling [[Drop of Honey]] and no creatures. Across the table my opponent had [[Kird Ape]] beside a [[Taiga]], and [[Savannah Lions]]. Both attackers had two power: the Taiga's Forest type kept the Ape at 2/3. Drop of Honey's ability triggered, and I chose the Lions from the tie for least power. They were destroyed without regeneration. The Ape survived that upkeep, so the enchantment was not an instant board wipe. I passed, knowing the next upkeep could remove the Ape too if no new smaller creature appeared.
articles.review: Kird Ape becomes 2/3 with Forest-type Taiga; Savannah Lions 2/1 both power 2. Drop untargeted tie chooses one at resolution. Only Lions die this upkeep, Ape stays. Controller creatureless.

articles.era: 1994 Worlds representative matchup under current Oracle rules
articles.matchup: U/W/G Stasis Control against red-green midrange
articles.title: I could keep the Ape only by staying tapped
articles.intro: Old Man of the Sea turns a tap ability into conditional creature theft: the target must have power no greater than Old Man's, and the control effect ends when the Old Man untaps or the power inequality breaks.
articles.lesson: Old Man of the Sea is a 2/3 with a tap-activated control ability and an optional skip of its own untap. The chosen target's power must be at most two when the ability resolves; untapping Old Man or raising the captured creature's power beyond its own ends control.
articles.origin: Susan Van Camp illustrated Old Man of the Sea for Arabian Nights. Its effect is more fragile than an Aura such as Control Magic because it depends both on the old creature remaining tapped and on a continual power comparison.
articles.technical: A Kird Ape with two power is a valid target for an Old Man with power two. A controller may skip untapping Old Man on their next untap step to keep the Ape; if Old Man untaps later or the Ape's power grows greater than two, control ends immediately.
articles.history: The existing archive labels Zak Dolan's U/W/G Stasis as a 1994 World Championship registration. The present theft scene is constructed; archival inclusion alone is not proof of any exact match.
articles.story: My [[Old Man of the Sea]] had been under my control since the start of the turn. I tapped it targeting an opposing [[Kird Ape]], whose [[Taiga]] made it a 2/3. The Ape had power two, no greater than the Old Man's power two, so the ability resolved and I gained control. During my next untap step I chose not to untap the Old Man. The stolen Ape remained on my side. If I let Old Man untap or my opponent raised the Ape's power above two, the theft would end. I could not simply forget the tap condition.
articles.review: Old Man 2/3 has continuous control while tapped and target power at most 2. Kird Ape + Taiga 2/3 qualifies. On controller next untap choose not to untap. Fictional opponent.

articles.era: 2015 Eternal Weekend Old School using modern triggers
articles.title: The Efreet took one, then dealt three
articles.intro: Serendib Efreet was an undercosted blue 3/4 flying attacker balanced by one damage to its controller each upkeep. It is not an automatic one-life payment when cast.
articles.lesson: The Efreet deals one damage to its controller at the beginning of that player's upkeep, and attacks for three flying combat damage if it has been under its controller's control since the start of their turn. Its Revised Edition green frame and alternate illustration were a printing error, not a change of color identity.
articles.origin: Anson Maddocks illustrated the original blue-framed Serendib Efreet for Arabian Nights in 1993. Revised's mistaken green frame and Ifh-Biff Efreet art should be distinguished from the original identity, not used as evidence that Serendib is a green card.
articles.technical: With the Efreet already controlled at the beginning of the turn, its one-damage upkeep trigger moves its controller from five to four life, then a legal attack deals three to an unblocked opponent. Its triggered self-damage still matters in games decided by racing.
articles.history: The 2015 Old School American Weenie archive credits Brian Fisher and includes the Efreet, providing an era-specific deck-pool reference without attributing a specific match or board state.
articles.story: My [[Serendib Efreet]] was ready at the beginning of my upkeep beside an untapped [[Island]], with [[Swords to Plowshares]] in hand. Its triggered ability dealt one damage to me, dropping my life total from five to four. I drew, declared the flying 3/4 as an attacker, and my opponent had no creature with flying or reach to block it. The Efreet dealt three combat damage, moving my opponent from six to three life. I had traded one point of life for a three-point attack this turn. The odd green-framed Revised printing on another table did not change my original blue card's cost or color.
articles.review: Efreet 3/4 with upkeep damage controller, 5->4. Flying unblocked 3 damage 6->3, creature began turn under controller. Revised misprint historically blue card with wrong green border/Ifh-Biff image.

articles.era: 1994 artifact strategy illustrated using current mana-pool rules
articles.title: The dead machine left four mana
articles.intro: Su-Chi is a four-mana 4/4 artifact creature whose death generates four colorless mana, a delayed resource that must be spent legally after the trigger resolves.
articles.lesson: Su-Chi adds four colorless mana when it dies. That happens on a triggered ability after death, not as part of casting or as a direct refund for an attempted spell. Before Magic removed mana burn in 2009, unspent mana could injure a player when a phase ended; that is not current gameplay.
articles.origin: Christopher Rush's Su-Chi debuted in Antiquities in 1994 as an efficient artifact body. The four-mana death payout shaped combat and sacrifice decisions as well as older mana-burn concerns.
articles.technical: If Su-Chi dies during a player's own main phase to instant removal, its controller may use the four generated colorless mana to cast a spell like Juggernaut when the stack is empty and timing permits. If it dies during an opponent's turn the controller cannot immediately cast a normal creature spell.
articles.history: The Workshop Prison archive is a clearly labeled curated Old School example; it illustrates artifact mana and creatures but cannot be recast as a named tournament registration.
articles.story: During my main phase my opponent used [[Disenchant]] on [[Su-Chi]], my 4/4 artifact creature. Su-Chi went to the graveyard, and its triggered ability put four colorless mana into my pool after resolving. When the stack was empty, I spent those four mana to cast [[Juggernaut]]. I had not received that mana when Su-Chi first entered the battlefield; the payout came only when it died. The sequence uses modern mana rules. At a historical 1994 table, leaving the mana unspent until the phase ended could instead have meant mana burn.
articles.review: Opponent casts Disenchant (instant) on my Su-Chi artifact creature during my main phase; after it dies, its death trigger adds four colorless. Stack empties, I may cast Juggernaut during own main phase with four mana. 1994 mana burn contrasted with modern rules; curated example not registered match.

articles.era: 2005 Standard-inspired demonstration using current counters rules
articles.matchup: Mono-Blue Tron against green creature acceleration
articles.title: Two counters paid for two creatures
articles.intro: Triskelion arrives as a six-mana artifact creature with three +1/+1 counters and can remove counters one by one to deal one damage to any target.
articles.lesson: Removing a +1/+1 counter is the activation cost of Triskelion's damage ability. Each activation deals one damage, and reducing the counters also reduces its own power and toughness. The machine begins as 4/4, not 1/1.
articles.origin: Douglas Shuler illustrated Triskelion for Antiquities. The counters turn a creature into an individually divisible damage source that can operate at instant speed even while newly controlled.
articles.technical: Triskelion begins as a 1/1 with three +1/+1 counters: 4/4. Two independent activations can remove two counters to deal one each to two 1/1 creatures, leaving Triskelion as 2/2. Those damage abilities do not require tapping.
articles.history: The archive's Antonino De Rosa Mono-Blue Tron list is a 2005 U.S. Nationals championship registration containing Triskelion. The green acceleration board in the scene is fictional.
articles.story: I had [[Triskelion]] on the battlefield as a 4/4, with three +1/+1 counters. My opponent controlled [[Llanowar Elves]] and [[Birds of Paradise]], both 1/1 creatures. I removed one counter to deal one damage to the Elves, then removed a second counter to deal one to Birds. Both creatures were destroyed by lethal damage. Triskelion now had one +1/+1 counter, making it a 2/2 rather than its original 4/4. I had not tapped it to fire either shot. I saved the final counter in case the opponent tried another creature before my next turn.
articles.review: 4/4 Triskelion starts with 3 counters on base 1/1; remove 2, each 1 damage to two 1/1s; 2/2 remains. No tap cost. 2005 deck includes Triskelion.

articles.era: 1994 Old School illustrated with modern upkeep rules
articles.matchup: Workshop Prison against ground-heavy red-green creatures
articles.title: One body became three flying bodies
articles.intro: Tetravus carries its own detachable +1/+1 counters: during upkeep the controller can convert them into flying Tetravite tokens or reabsorb their own tokens.
articles.lesson: Tetravus enters with three +1/+1 counters and has flying. At the beginning of its controller's upkeep it can remove any number of those counters to create that many 1/1 flying Tetravite artifact creature tokens, or sacrifice Tetravites it controls to put counters back on Tetravus.
articles.origin: Mark Tedin illustrated Tetravus for Antiquities. It transforms a single efficient artifact flyer into a swarm across future upkeeps, changing how board wipes, blocks and removal trade against one another.
articles.technical: With a base 1/1 and three +1/+1 counters, Tetravus starts as 4/4. Removing two counters at an upkeep produces two 1/1 flying Tetravites and leaves Tetravus 2/2. On a future upkeep its controller may choose to sacrifice Tetravites to restore counters, rather than freely recombining at instant speed.
articles.history: The Workshop Prison archive is a curated Old School model rather than a verified event registration. Its Tetravus placement demonstrates an artifact-finisher role but not a particular player's tournament actions.
articles.story: At the beginning of my upkeep, [[Tetravus]] still had all three +1/+1 counters and was a 4/4 flyer. I chose to remove two counters, creating two 1/1 flying Tetravite artifact creature tokens. Tetravus was now a 2/2 flyer, and I had three bodies instead of one. My opponent's [[Kird Ape]] and [[Juggernaut]] were formidable on the ground, but neither could block a flyer without help. I could not put the tokens back onto Tetravus whenever I wished; a later upkeep would offer that choice again.
articles.review: Tetravus 1/1 plus3 counters 4/4. Remove2 at own upkeep -> 2/2 + two 1/1 flying Tetravite tokens. Ground Ape/Juggernaut can't block flyers. Later upkeep permits reattachment.

articles.title: Two sacrificed artifacts changed the clock
articles.intro: Atog is a two-mana 1/2 whose free activated ability sacrifices an artifact to give it +2/+2 until end of turn. The resource conversion is powerful but permanent and not reversible.
articles.lesson: Each sacrificed artifact is paid as a cost, giving Atog +2/+2 through end of turn. From 1/2, two sacrifices make it 5/6. Sacrificing an artifact land does not make another land drop available.
articles.origin: Jesper Myrfors illustrated Atog for Antiquities in 1994. Artifact-focused sets later provided unusually convenient sacrifice material, but the spell's printed red mana identity and activation rule remained intact.
articles.technical: On an unblocked Atog with opponent at five, sacrificing two artifact permanents during combat makes a 5/6 that can deal lethal five combat damage. The artifacts are sacrificed immediately as activation costs, so removing Atog in response does not bring them back.
articles.history: The archive identifies Kamiel Cornelissen's 2004 World Championship list with Atog and Mirrodin-era artifacts. The exact two-sacrifice kill is fictional, not a described match from that event.
articles.story: My [[Atog]] attacked while my opponent sat at five life with no blocker. Before combat damage I sacrificed [[Ornithopter]] to its ability, making Atog 3/4. I then sacrificed an [[Seat of the Synod]], an artifact land I already controlled, and Atog became 5/6 until end of turn. Those two artifacts went to the graveyard as activation costs. When combat damage was dealt, the five power was lethal. I did not get an extra land play for sacrificing Seat of the Synod, and losing the artifact land would matter if the attack failed.
articles.review: Atog 1/2 + 2*2/+2 = 5/6; sacrifices Ornithopter + Seat of Synod are ability costs. 5 combat damage lethal to 5-life opponent; opponent no blocker.

articles.title: A free Thopter made Frogmite cheaper
articles.intro: Ornithopter has no mana cost to pay and almost no natural offense, but its artifact type makes every affinity calculation, sacrifice engine and artifact-counting board state different.
articles.lesson: Ornithopter is a 0/2 flying artifact creature that costs {0}. Casting it uses normal spell timing and the stack; once it resolves, its artifact status contributes to affinity for artifacts even though Ornithopter itself generated no mana.
articles.origin: Amy Weber illustrated the original Ornithopter in Antiquities. It became a defining raw-material card as later artifact-count payoffs made a free creature worth a slot.
articles.technical: With two artifact lands and Ornithopter on the battlefield, Frogmite's affinity for artifacts reduces its {4} generic cost by three, leaving {1}. One artifact land can tap for mana to pay that residual cost, while still counting as an artifact even after tapping.
articles.history: Ben Stark's Pro Tour Kobe 2004 Affinity archive illustrates the relationship between free artifacts and Frogmite; the specific hand and board are reconstructed rather than attributed event footage.
articles.story: I had [[Seat of the Synod]] and [[Vault of Whispers]] on the battlefield and no creature yet. During my main phase I cast [[Ornithopter]] for zero mana. It resolved as a 0/2 flyer and became my third artifact. [[Frogmite]] cost four generic mana normally, but affinity for artifacts reduced that by three. I tapped Seat of the Synod to pay the remaining one mana and cast Frogmite. Tapping the artifact land did not stop it from counting for affinity. My opponent still faced two new creatures, even though I had spent only one mana.
articles.review: Two artifact lands + Ornithopter after resolution =3 artifacts. Frogmite {4} affinity reduces to {1}. Seat of Synod taps to pay blue amount generic, still artifact. Zero mana spell uses stack; user controls newly played creature cannot attack this turn.

articles.title: The Cane left; the library returned
articles.intro: Feldon's Cane is a one-mana artifact with a tap-and-exile activated ability that shuffles the controller's graveyard into their library, trading the artifact permanently for future draw steps.
articles.lesson: Exiling Feldon's Cane is part of the activation cost, so it is gone before the shuffle ability resolves. The ability shuffles only its controller's graveyard, not the opponent's, and does not put the Cane itself into the library.
articles.origin: Mark Tedin illustrated Feldon's Cane for Antiquities. The card offered resource recycling for lengthy control games without producing immediate extra cards in hand.
articles.technical: When an activated Cane has been tapped and exiled as costs, the controller shuffles the remaining graveyard into their library on resolution. If the ability is countered, the Cane remains exiled and the graveyard is not shuffled. It provides no extra draw by itself.
articles.history: Matt Place's 1996 Turbo Stasis list includes Feldon's Cane among the card-draw and control infrastructure. The narrated low-library scene is representative, not a recorded Nationals game.
articles.story: I had only three cards left in my library, and [[Howling Mine]] was making each draw step dangerous. My [[Feldon's Cane]] and [[Stasis]] had been on the battlefield since earlier turns. I tapped it and exiled it to activate the ability. When that ability resolved, I shuffled the cards in my graveyard back into my library. The Cane itself was not among them; it was already exiled as part of the cost. My opponent still controlled their own graveyard, untouched. I had bought more possible draw steps, not drawn an extra card or recovered the Cane.
articles.review: Feldon's Cane tap+exile activation costs paid before resolving. Only controller graveyard shuffled into their library; Cane exiled does not return. Howling Mine adds draws. 1996 deck contains both.
